name: length+
summary: The length of a proper list, or #f if the list is circular -- the length verb that is safe to call on anything.
explanation: Plain length walks a list until it reaches the end. On a circular list there is no end, so length does not return an answer, it fails to terminate -- and a program that hangs tells you nothing about where it hung. length+ exists to make that case reportable instead of fatal. It walks the list with two cursors, one moving one pair at a time and one moving two, and if the fast cursor ever catches the slow one the list must contain a cycle, so it answers #f. Otherwise it answers the count, exactly as length would. The cost is the same order as length -- a constant factor more work, no extra allocation -- so the price of safety is small. Read the return type as the whole point: an integer means 'proper list of this length', and #f means 'this list has no length', which is a genuinely different fact from 'this list is empty'. Any code that has to accept a list from somewhere it does not control should be measuring with length+ and branching on #f, not calling length and hoping.

examples.note: 3 -- on a proper list it is just length.
(empty 0 three 3 nested 2) -- it counts top-level pairs, so a list of two lists has length 2, not 4.

examples.code:
(define (describe xs)
  (let ((n (length+ xs)))
    (cond ((not n) 'circular)
          ((= n 0) 'empty)
          ((= n 1) 'singleton)
          (else n))))
(display (map describe (list '() '(a) '(a b c) '((x)))))
(newline)
examples.note: (empty singleton 3 singleton) -- one call covers every shape, and the #f branch is written even though these inputs never take it.

caveats: It answers #f for a circular list, and #f is not a number. (+ 1 (length+ xs)) raises on the very input length+ was called to survive -- always branch on the result.
#f means 'no length', not 'length zero'. The empty list answers 0. Confusing the two inverts the meaning of every guard built on it.
It counts top-level pairs only. A list of lists has the length of the outer list; nothing is flattened and nothing is counted recursively.
It is not a circularity test that you should read as one. It answers #f for circular input, but a verb named circular-list? states that intent directly and is what a reader expects to see.
It costs a constant factor more than length because of the second cursor. On a hot path over lists you already know are proper, plain length is the honest choice.
usecases: Measuring a list that arrived from outside the program, where a cycle is possible and a hang is not acceptable.
Writing a total 'describe this value' routine that has a branch for every shape a list can have.
Guarding an algorithm that requires a finite list, by refusing up front rather than looping forever inside.

learn.concept: A total function returns something for every input; making the failure case a VALUE rather than a hang is what lets the caller handle it.
learn.progression: Call length on a proper list, then call length+ and see the same number. Then ask what length would do on a list with no end, and notice that 'crash' would have been a better outcome than what it actually does. #f is the third answer that makes the question answerable at all.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (batch-report jobs)
  (let ((n (length+ jobs)))
    (cond ((not n) (list 'status 'rejected 'reason 'unbounded))
          ((= n 0) (list 'status 'idle 'jobs 0))
          (else (list 'status 'ready 'jobs n)))))
(display (list (batch-report '()) (batch-report '(a b c d))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (cardinality s)
  (let ((n (length+ s)))
    (if n n 'infinite)))
(display (list 'empty-set (cardinality '())
               'singleton (cardinality '(a))
               'finite (cardinality '(a b c d e))
               'sum (+ (cardinality '(a b)) (cardinality '(c d e)))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A job runner is handed a list of work from an untrusted caller and has to report how much there is. Candidates: length+ (one pass, answers a number for anything finite and #f for anything circular, so the runner can refuse rather than hang), length (correct and faster on proper lists, and on a circular one the process stops responding with no message anywhere), list? followed by length (two passes, and list? has the same termination question unless it is itself cycle-safe), a manual loop with a step counter and a cap (works, but the cap is a magic number and a legitimate long list gets rejected), catching an exception (nothing is thrown -- the failure mode is non-termination, not an error, which is exactly why length+ has to exist). length+ is the only candidate that turns the bad case into data.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: a batch report with a branch for every outcome, including the rejection path that the good inputs never reach but that has to be written. math: the same call read as the cardinality of a finite set, where #f would mean the set is not finite and where the counts add across disjoint parts. cs: the direct comparison showing length+ and length agree on proper lists, and that the empty list answers 0 rather than #f -- the distinction the whole verb rests on.
row-2-audit.meta: Why length+ and not length: the choice is not about correctness on good input, where they are identical. It is about which failure the program prefers -- a value it can branch on, or a hang with no diagnostic.
row-2-audit.eng: A service that hangs is harder to debug than one that refuses, because the refusal has a reason attached and the hang has a stack trace at best.
row-2-audit.math: Cardinality is defined for finite sets and undefined otherwise. Representing 'undefined' as a distinguished value is what makes the function total.
row-2-audit.cs: 0 and #f are both falsy in many languages and neither is falsy in Scheme. That is why this verb can return both and stay unambiguous.

row-3-dimension.setup: Asking how many things there are, in a way that survives the possibility that the answer does not exist.

rungs.domain: counting samples in a recorded signal before computing its mean amplitude
rungs.code:
(define (mean-amplitude samples)
  (let ((n (length+ samples)))
    (cond ((not n) 'unbounded)
          ((= n 0) 'no-samples)
          (else (/ (apply + samples) n)))))
(display (list 'recorded (mean-amplitude '(2 4 6 8))
               'silence (mean-amplitude '())
               'single (mean-amplitude '(7))))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a scheduler admitting a workload only if it is provably finite
rungs.code:
(define (admit workload budget)
  (let ((n (length+ workload)))
    (cond ((not n) (list 'refused 'unbounded))
          ((> n budget) (list 'refused 'over-budget n))
          (else (list 'admitted n (- budget n))))))
(display (list (admit '(a b c) 5) (admit '(a b c d e f) 5) (admit '() 5)))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: As bare structure it is a count with three sizes and nothing at stake. Applied to a recorded signal it becomes a divisor: the mean cannot be computed without it, and the two cases where there is no usable count -- no samples at all, and no bound -- are not the same case and must not collapse into one. In a scheduler it becomes an admission decision, where the count is compared against a budget and 'unbounded' is a refusal reason on equal footing with 'too big'. The call is identical throughout; what climbs is what the number is FOR -- reporting, then dividing, then deciding -- and correspondingly how much a missing answer costs.
row-3-dimension.meta: The ladder is really about the #f branch. On rung one it is invisible, on rung two it is one of three arms of a cond, and on rung three it is a first-class refusal reason that a caller reads. The verb only earns its extra cursor at the top of the ladder.
row-3-dimension.eng: Dividing by a count you did not check is how a mean becomes a division-by-zero in production. The empty case and the unbounded case both have to be caught, and they are different.
row-3-dimension.math: The arithmetic mean is defined on non-empty finite sequences. Both halves of that precondition are exactly what length+ reports on.
row-3-dimension.cs: Admission control means refusing work you cannot bound. A workload whose size cannot be measured is unbounded by definition, and admitting it is the same mistake as admitting an infinite one.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (agrees-with-length? xs)
  (eqv? (length+ xs) (length xs)))
(display (map agrees-with-length?
              (list '() '(a) '(a b) '(a b c d e) '((x y) (z)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (additive-over-append? a b)
  (= (length+ (append a b)) (+ (length+ a) (length+ b))))
(display (map (lambda (p) (apply additive-over-append? p))
              (list (list '() '()) (list '() '(1 2)) (list '(1) '(2 3)) (list '(1 2 3) '()) (list '(1 2) '(3 4)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (answer-is-a-count? xs)
  (let ((n (length+ xs)))
    (and (integer? n) (>= n 0) (if (null? xs) (= n 0) (> n 0)))))
(display (map answer-is-a-count? (list '() '(a) '(a b c) '((a)) '(#f #f))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: On every proper list length+ gives exactly what length gives; the count is additive over append; and the answer is always a non-negative integer that is 0 for the empty list and positive otherwise -- never #f, because none of these lists are circular.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all proper lists xs. length+(xs) = length(xs); for all proper a, b. length+(append(a, b)) = length+(a) + length+(b); and length+(xs) is an integer >= 0 with length+(xs) = 0 iff xs = ()
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims covering compatibility, structure and typing. What would falsify them: a cycle detector that fired on a long proper list (the compatibility test would disagree), a count that was off by one at a join (the additivity test would fail on the two-non-empty case), or an answer of #f where a number was due (the typing test would fail). The list containing two #f values is in the third program on purpose: it is where an implementation that confused a falsy ELEMENT with a falsy RESULT would break. Circularity itself cannot be tested here without constructing a cycle, which is the one input a deterministic printed program cannot display.
row-4-proof.eng: Agreement with length is the migration guarantee. It is what says you can replace one with the other without re-reading the call site.
row-4-proof.math: Additivity over append is the statement that length is a monoid homomorphism from lists-under-append to numbers-under-addition, which is why splitting a list never changes the total.
row-4-proof.cs: Distinguishing a false element from a false result is why the return type has to be checked, not just truth-tested. (if (length+ xs) ...) is right; (if (car xs) ...) is a different question entirely.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (safe-count xs) (length+ xs))
(define (queue-report queues)
  (let ((counts (map safe-count queues)))
    (if (member #f counts)
        (list 'status 'unmeasurable)
        (list 'queues (length counts)
              'total (apply + counts)
              'deepest (apply max counts)
              'idle (length (filter zero? counts))))))
(display (queue-report '((a b c) () (d) (e f))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (size s) (length+ s))
(define (partition-check whole parts)
  (let ((n (size whole)) (ns (map size parts)))
    (list 'whole n 'parts ns 'sums-to (apply + ns) 'consistent (= n (apply + ns)))))
(display (partition-check '(1 2 3 4 5 6) '((1 2) (3 4 5) (6))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (measured xs) (length+ xs))
(define (histogram lists)
  (fold (lambda (xs acc)
          (let ((n (measured xs)))
            (if n (alist-cons n (+ 1 (or (and (assv n acc) (cdr (assv n acc))) 0)) (alist-delete n acc)) acc)))
        '() lists))
(display (histogram '((a) (b c) (d) (e f g) (h i) (j))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: length+ measures a list and answers #f rather than hanging when it cannot.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: safe-count is one call; queue-report maps it across every queue and then aggregates -- total depth, deepest queue, how many are idle -- and the one #f anywhere collapses the whole report to 'unmeasurable' rather than poisoning an average. math: size is one call; partition-check uses it on the whole and on each part and asserts that the parts sum to the whole, which is how you verify a partition without comparing elements at all. cs: measured is one call; histogram folds it over a list of lists and tallies how many lists had each length, turning a pile of sequences into a distribution.
row-5-emergence.meta: The composition is always measure-then-aggregate, and the interesting part is what happens to #f under aggregation. Summing it would raise; averaging it would be nonsense; so the eng version checks for it before aggregating and the cs version skips it. Deciding that policy is the real work, and it only exists because the base verb can fail with a value.
row-5-emergence.eng: One unmeasurable queue makes the total meaningless. Reporting 'unmeasurable' is more useful than reporting a total that silently excluded something.
row-5-emergence.math: Checking that the parts sum to the whole is a necessary condition for a partition, not a sufficient one -- it catches double-counting and omission but not overlap.
row-5-emergence.cs: A length histogram is the cheapest possible profile of a nested structure, and it is often enough to tell a balanced tree from a degenerate one without ever looking at a key.
